subject: Climate & Environment
title: The E-Waste Mountain
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The E-Waste Mountain.

hook.text: The world generates 62 million tons of electronic waste per year. Less than 20% is recycled.

buildup.text: Phones, laptops, TVs, and appliances are replaced faster than ever before.

discovery.text: E-waste contains gold, silver, copper, and rare earths — worth over $60 billion per year.

twist.text: Most e-waste is dumped in developing countries where children pick it apart by hand.

climax.text: The toxic metals inside — lead, mercury, cadmium — poison soil and water for generations.

punchline.text: Our newest technology becomes someone else's oldest poison.

quiz.question: How much electronic waste does the world generate annually?

details.summary: The world generates over 62 million tonnes of electronic waste per year, and less than 20 percent is formally recycled. Discarded phones, computers, and appliances contain valuable metals like gold, copper, and rare earths, but also hazardous materials like lead, mercury, and cadmium.
details.whyItMatters: E-waste is the fastest growing waste stream globally. It represents both a massive resource loss and a toxic threat when improperly handled in developing countries.
takeaways: Over 62 million tonnes of e-waste is generated annually
Less than 20 percent is formally recycled worldwide
E-waste contains both valuable and hazardous materials

faq.question: What valuable materials are in e-waste?
faq.answer: A tonne of circuit boards contains roughly 800 times more gold than a tonne of gold ore. E-waste also contains copper, silver, palladium, platinum, and rare earth elements. The total value of raw materials in global e-waste exceeds $60 billion annually.

faq.question: Why is so little e-waste recycled?
faq.answer: Recycling electronics is complex and costly, requiring specialized dismantling. Many consumers hoard old devices or throw them in regular trash. Collection systems are inadequate, and informal recyclers in developing countries process e-waste unsafely for quick profit.
